Subunit 3: Reading and Judging Charts

About 15 minutes · 5 short sections

Charts are everywhere: in the news, on social media, in reports, and in your own assignments. A chart can make a pattern clear in seconds. It can also mislead, even when every number in it is correct.

How this page works

  • Each section scrolls. When you finish one, press Next section at the bottom.
  • Most sections end with a quick question. These are not graded. Any answer unlocks the next section, and then you’ll see the correct answer and why.
  • You can go back to any section you’ve finished using the menu at the top.

By the end, you’ll be able to:

  1. Check a chart before trusting it, and sum it up in one sentence.
  2. Spot a chart that doesn’t fit its data.
  3. Judge a chart with five simple rules, including why bars start at zero.
  4. Pick the right type of chart for a question.
  5. Tell the difference between a count and a rate.

Section 3.1

Read a chart before you believe it

Charts feel like facts. Before you trust one, check what it actually tells you. Take a look at this chart.

Five things to check. Click each card to see what the posted version is missing.

① Title

What is this chart about?

Missing. With no title, you have to guess the topic. A good title tells you the point of the chart, not just the topic.

② Axes, units, labels

What is measured, and which line is which?

Missing. Is 40 dollars, thousands of dollars, or a percent? And there’s no way to tell which line is which country.

③ Source

Who collected these numbers?

Missing. Without a source you can’t check the data, or know whether the source has a stake in the story.

④ Time period

Which years?

Missing. A trend over 5 years can look very different from the same trend over 25 years.

⑤ What’s left out

Which cases or years aren’t shown?

Ask anyway. Even the fixed chart shows only three countries. Choosing which cases to show is a choice, and it shapes the story.

Now switch to ✔ The fixed chart above and see how each problem was fixed.

One chart, one sentence

A good chart can be summed up in one clear takeaway sentence. Here’s how the fixed chart gets there:

Question How did income per person in the U.S., Canada, and Mexico compare from 1990 to 2014? Data GDP per capita from POLI-LIT Chart A line chart, because it shows change over time Takeaway One sentence that answers the question

Quick check

Which is the best takeaway sentence for the fixed chart?

  1. This chart shows GDP data for three countries.
  2. The x-axis is the year and the y-axis is GDP per capita.
  3. Mexico was poorer because its government was less democratic.
  4. The U.S. and Canada stayed far richer per person than Mexico from 1990 to 2014, and the gap grew.

Option 4 answers the question with what the chart actually shows. Options 1 and 2 only describe the chart. Option 3 claims a cause, but the chart has no democracy data, and even if it did, a pattern alone doesn’t prove a cause (remember Lecture 2).

Section 3.2

When a chart doesn’t fit the data

A chart can be made without a single error and still be a bad chart. This one shows how many intergovernmental organizations (IGOs) each country in the Middle East and North Africa belonged to in 2014. Is it a good chart?

Why the pie doesn’t work:

  • The data aren’t parts of one whole. A pie shows shares of a total, like the share of students in each class year. Each country’s IGO count is its own total, so “Egypt’s slice of the pie” means nothing.
  • Too many slices. Pies work with about five or six categories at most. With 14, the slices look alike and the colors are hard to match to the legend.
  • No clear takeaway. You can’t easily tell who has the most or the fewest.

Switch to ✔ Fixed: bar chart. Sorted bars make the comparison easy, and the title states the point.

Quick check

Why is a pie chart the wrong choice for these data?

  1. Pie charts can’t show more than three colors
  2. Each country’s IGO count is its own total, not a share of one whole
  3. Pie charts can only be used for money
  4. The numbers are too large for a pie chart

A pie only makes sense when the slices add up to a meaningful whole. These counts don’t, so a bar chart that compares them side by side is the better fit.

Section 3.3

Five rules for a good chart

  1. A title that states the point, not just the topic.
  2. Labeled axes with units (dollars? percent? a 0–1 score?).
  3. A caption with the source and the years.
  4. Keep it simple: no 3-D effects, no extra decoration, readable colors.
  5. Bars start at zero. A bar’s length stands for its value, so cutting off the bottom distorts the comparison.

The fixed charts in 3.1 and 3.2 follow rules 1–4. Rule 5 is the one most often broken, so try it yourself. This chart shows each region’s average Gender Equality Index (0–1, higher = more equal) in 2014. Switch between the two versions.

In the cut version, Middle East & North Africa’s bar almost disappears, and W. Europe & N. America’s bar looks about 30 times longer. In fact, 0.92 is less than twice 0.51.

Line charts are different. A line chart shows change, not length, so it’s fine for its axis to zoom in, as long as the axis is clearly labeled.

Quick check

The data are the same, but the axis now starts at 0.5. What changed?

  1. The regions’ scores went down
  2. The data source changed
  3. Only how big the differences look
  4. Nothing at all

Every number is the same. Cutting the axis only makes the gaps look much bigger. That’s why bar charts should start at zero.

Section 3.4

Which chart for which question?

Different charts answer different questions. Match the chart to the question you’re asking and the type of data you have (remember levels of measurement from Subunit 2).

ChartData it fitsQuestion it answers
Pie1 categorical variable, few categoriesWhat share of the whole is each part?
Histogram1 numeric variableHow are the values spread out? Where do they cluster?
Bar1 categorical + 1 numericWhich group is bigger or smaller?
LineTime + 1 numericHow did it change over time?
Scatter2 numeric variablesDo two things move together?

Histogram vs. bar chart. They look alike but aren’t the same. A histogram groups numbers into ranges, so its bars touch (like the GDP histogram in Subunit 2). A bar chart compares separate groups, so its bars have gaps (like the regions in 3.3).

Matching game

Pick the best chart for each question.

How has Mexico’s democracy score changed since 1990?

Change over time → line.

Do richer countries tend to have higher democracy scores?

Two numeric variables moving together → scatter.

Which region has the highest average gender equality?

Comparing groups → bar.

How is GDP per capita spread across all countries?

The spread of one numeric variable → histogram.

What share of SAEL 200 students are in each class year?

Parts of one whole, with only four categories → pie (a bar chart would also work).

Section 3.5

Counts vs. rates

A count is a raw total. A rate divides that total by something, such as the number of people, so places of different sizes can be compared fairly.

Here are traffic deaths in 2024 for California and South Carolina. Switch between the two versions.

California has about seven times as many people as South Carolina (39.4 million vs. 5.5 million), so of course it has more deaths in total. The rate asks a fairer question: out of every 100,000 people, how many died? By that measure, South Carolina’s roads were far deadlier.

Key idea. When a headline says a place has “the most” of something, ask: is that a count or a rate? Big places usually have the biggest counts.

Quick check

A headline says California has the most traffic deaths of these two states. Does that mean its roads are the most dangerous?

  1. Yes, more deaths means more dangerous roads
  2. Not necessarily. You need the rate, because California has far more people
  3. Yes, because the numbers come from a trusted source
  4. No, because the data are wrong

The count is correct, but it mostly reflects California’s size. The rate (deaths per 100,000 people) shows that South Carolina’s was almost twice as high.

✅ You’ve finished Subunit 3

Next: continue to Subunit 4, Data Ethics. After Subunit 4, complete Check-in 2 on Blackboard. It covers Subunits 3 and 4 and is graded on completion.

Before you go, a quick recap:

  • Check the title, axes and units, source, years, and what’s left out before trusting a chart.
  • Sum up a chart in one takeaway sentence, without claiming more than it shows.
  • Match the chart to the data and the question.
  • Bars start at zero.
  • Ask whether a number is a count or a rate.
